# De-escalation

`customer_support.customer_communication.de_escalation` · v1.0.0 · **draft**

**Why is this person angry, and what would make them feel in control again?**


> Bringing the temperature of a contact down far enough that the real problem can actually be worked, and doing it without buying quiet with promises the queue cannot keep. The work is rarely about the fault: it is about the uncertainty and the sense of not being heard that grew around the fault while nobody said anything. So de-escalation is a communication discipline rather than a concession budget, and it is finished when the customer can predict what happens next — not when they stop writing in capitals. A customer who goes quiet because they have given up looks identical, on every dashboard support owns, to one who has been recovered.

## Expertise applied


## Outcomes

- The customer's own account of what happened has been played back to them in their words, before any explanation of ours was offered.
- The thing they are actually aggrieved about is named and is distinct from the defect — usually the not-knowing, the repeating, or the being handed around.
- A specific next contact exists: a named owner, a stated time, and a commitment that it happens whether or not there is news.
- Nothing was promised that the queue cannot deliver. An expectation set to end an uncomfortable exchange is a future escalation with a date on it.
- The customer can state, unprompted, what happens next and who is doing it. If they ask again, de-escalation has not happened yet.
- Where the contact still needs a different owner, it moved as a real escalation with a receiving name — not as a way of making the anger someone else's.
- The grievance is recorded separately from the ticket outcome, so a resolved ticket with an unrepaired relationship is still visible downstream.


## Failure modes

- Defending the company in the first sentence. Everything after it is heard as continuation of the defence, including the parts intended as apology. This is the characteristic failure of the capability and it is usually committed by the most technically competent agent on the team, because they can see immediately that the customer's account is inaccurate.
- Going quiet in order to come back with something concrete. Silence is itself a message and it is almost always the worst one available: the customer fills the gap and the story they write is worse than anything we would have had to admit.
- Explaining before acknowledging. Not a sequencing preference — an explanation offered first is processed as a rebuttal, and a person who is being rebutted cannot absorb the content of the rebuttal.
- A sincere apology carrying no next time. It asks the customer to trust our feelings when what they need is something they can check against a calendar.
- Matching the customer's emotion rather than their urgency. An anxious reply to an angry one confirms their fear that nobody here is in control, and that fear is the actual engine of the escalation.
- Offering compensation before acknowledgement. It teaches the account that the fastest route to being taken seriously is to be expensive, and it reads as buying silence even when it is generous.
- Escalating to make the anger stop rather than because a different owner can do something the current one cannot. It buys quiet this week and installs anger as the routing mechanism for every future contact.
- Correcting the customer's version of events while they are still hot. The inaccuracy is real and correcting it is a later conversation; done now it costs the whole relationship to win a detail.
- Reading softened tone as resolution. Tone softens in resignation as often as in reassurance, and the resigned customer is the one who does not renew.
- Over-explaining root cause to someone who only wants to know whether they can work tomorrow. Depth of explanation is a service to the explainer here.
- Passing the contact between agents so each can bring fresh eyes. Reassignment is invisible to us and highly visible to them, and every handover resets the retelling.
- Treating an angry public post and an angry private email as the same event. The audience changes what the customer needs from the reply, and it changes nothing about what we owe them privately.


## KPIs

| KPI | Unit | Direction | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| time_to_first_acknowledgement | hours | lower_is_better | Deliberately not first response. Acknowledgement is the message that names what happened without needing an answer, and it is the clock that actually governs temperature.  |
| promised_update_hit_rate | percent | higher_is_better | Share of committed next-contact times that were met. The most predictive single number in this capability, because it is the one the customer is also keeping.  |
| longest_silence_gap | hours | lower_is_better | Longest stretch with no outbound message while the contact was open and hot. |
| reassignment_count | count | lower_is_better | Owners the customer has had to explain themselves to. Each one resets the retelling. |
| repeat_contact_rate | percent | lower_is_better | Customers who wrote again before we wrote to them. A direct measure of unmet reassurance. |
| escalation_rate_after_heated_contact | percent | lower_is_better | Rising here alongside a flat defect rate means anger is functioning as the routing mechanism and the organisation has taught it.  |
| sentiment_recovery_rate | percent | higher_is_better | Contacts that started hot and ended measurably better. Weak on its own — resignation reads as recovery. |
| post_recovery_retention | percent | higher_is_better | Whether recovered accounts actually stayed. The only measure that distinguishes de-escalation from exhaustion, and the only reason to trust the sentiment number above it.  |
| goodwill_concession_rate | percent | target_band | Credits and refunds issued per heated contact. A band, not a direction — near zero means agents have no room to act, and high means the team is buying quiet instead of earning it.  |

> The load-bearing content here is failure_modes and the heuristics' `why` clauses, not the outcomes. Note also what is absent: no thresholds for how long a silence is too long, no definition of what counts as heated, no escalation trigger. Those are Layer 4's arithmetic and they belong in the pack manifest. What makes this capability hard to run today is upstream of that — there is no angry_language observation kind, no cancellation_threat, no escalation signal in the shipped substrate, so nothing in this file can currently be fired automatically. That gap is the point of vocabulary.yaml planned_substrate and is tracked there rather than papered over here by binding heat to derived.sentiment, which measures a different thing.
